titleStmt.title: Good Gig, Bad Gig: Autonomy and Algorithmic Control in the Global Gig Economy
titleStmt.author: Alex J. Wood
Mark Graham
Vili Lehdonvirta
Isis Hjorth

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Good Gig, Bad Gig: Autonomy and Algorithmic Control in the Global Gig Economy

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: job quality in the remote gig economy - digital services sold through online labour platforms by workers in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa to clients in high-income countries
span.quote: This article evaluates the job quality of work in the remote gig economy. Such work consists of the remote provision of a wide variety of digital services mediated by online labour platforms.

span.label: what the job quality of remote gig work is, and which organisational forms of control explain the commonalities across platforms and countries
span.quote: The second aim of this article is therefore to identify the organisational forms (such as Taylorist and algorithmic controls) that could explain commonalities in the quality remote gig work across the platforms and countries that we study, and how these organisational forms are shaped by power and technology.

span.label: evidence that algorithmic control, unlike Taylorism, delivers high autonomy AND low pay, isolation and overwork at once; and the identification of platform reputation as a symbolic form of marketplace bargaining power
span.quote: The identification of the ‘symbolic power’ ( Thompson, 1991) of platform reputations as an emerging form of marketplace bargaining power is an important contribution of this article.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Despite varying country contexts and types of work, we show that algorithmic control is central to the operation of online labour platforms. Algorithmic management techniques tend to offer workers high levels of flexibility, autonomy, task variety and complexity. However, these mechanisms of control can also result in low pay, social isolation, working unsocial and irregular hours, overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion.

span.label: remote gig workers experiencing genuine autonomy and severe overwork as two effects of the same system of control
span.quote: The autonomy resulting from algorithmic control can lead to overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion as a consequence of the weak structural power of workers vis-a-vis clients.

span.label: 107 face-to-face semi-structured interviews across six countries over seven months of fieldwork, coded by theory elaboration, plus a non-probability purposive survey of 679 platform workers
span.term: 107 face-to-face semi-structured interviews across six countries over seven months of fieldwork, coded by theory elaboration, plus a non-probability purposive survey of 679 platform workers
span.quote: Our analysis is primarily based on face-to-face semi-structured interviews with 107 workers. The worker informants consist of 36 workers in Southeast Asia (SEA, comprising 12 in the Philippines, five in Malaysia and 19 in Vietnam), and 71 in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA, comprising 29 in Kenya, 23 in Nigeria and 19 in South Africa).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: CONTROL AT THE END OF THE LABOUR PROCESS, NOT DURING IT. Only the delivered product is judged, so the worker is genuinely free in method, hours and place - and the same fact means the rating that governs all future work is assigned after the work is done and cannot be argued with
span.quote: What is notable about this algorithmic system of control in terms of job quality, compared to Taylorist forms of informational control, is that control operated at the end of the labour process rather than during it.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NON-PROXIMITY DEFEATS SUPERVISION AND THE RATING RESTORES IT: clients in high-income countries cannot watch workers in SEA and SSA, so direct monitoring fails - and platform rating and ranking overcome exactly the spatial and temporal barriers that defeated it
span.quote: This weak structural power is an outcome of platform-based rating and ranking systems enabling a form of control which is able to overcome the spatial and temporal barriers that non-proximity places on the effectiveness of direct labour process surveillance and supervision.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: RANKING IS THE SANCTION: platforms do not dismiss low-rated workers, they filter work away from them, so the penalty is invisible, gradual and unappealable - continuing on the platform simply stops being a viable living
span.quote: online labour platforms, instead, use algorithms to filter work away from those with low ratings, thus making continuing on the platform a less viable means of making a living.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: DIRECT MONITORING WAS EASILY CIRCUMVENTED - keystroke counts and screenshots were worked around by timing and by a second monitor - which is why the reputational mechanism, not the surveillance mechanism, is the effective one
span.quote: For instance, frequencies of workers’ keyboard presses and mouse movements were tracked and shots taken of their screens. However, these monitoring mechanisms were easily circumvented.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WORKERS WELCOMED THE MONITORING because the platform guaranteed payment for monitored work: surveillance was traded for protection against wage theft, so the same mechanism is a safeguard and a control depending on who is short of power
span.quote: In fact, the monitoring was often welcomed by workers, because the platform guaranteed payments for monitored work, protecting workers from non-payment and wage theft

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: FORMAL CONTROL WITHOUT REAL CHOICE: workers hold genuine authority over where and when they work and have little real alternative to home and to unsocial hours, because client demand and weak structural power set the terms
span.quote: while algorithmic control provides remote gig workers with formal control over where they work, workers may have little real choice but to work from home, and this can lead to a lack of social contact and feelings of social isolation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN UNREGULATED GLOBAL OVERSUPPLY OF LABOUR is what the platform connects clients to, and it is the source of the weak structural power that turns autonomy into overwork
span.quote: Online labour platforms thus facilitate clients in connecting with a largely unregulated global oversupply of labour.

span.label: probability sampling is stated to be impossible on an online labour platform, because the chance of any member seeing the survey task is unequal and unknown
span.quote: Probability sampling is not possible through an online labour platform (at least without the platform owner’s collaboration), because the probability of members seeing and responding to the survey task is unequal and unknown.

span.label: response rates were 30% and 7% on the two platforms, which the authors call low by conventional social survey standards
span.quote: The response rates to the invitations were 30% and 7% on the two platforms respectively, which are low by conventional social survey standards, but an improvement on entirely self-selecting online surveys.

span.label: the sample resembles a quota sample except that subsample sizes were not predefined - they depended on how easy each subpopulation was to find
span.quote: The result is similar to a stratified or quota sample, except that the subsample sizes were not predefined but depended on how easy or difficult it was to find members of each subpopulation on the platform.

span.label: the population of remote gig workers is called an ambiguous concept, since engagement runs from a registered account to a full-time income and changes over time; the authors define it by a work threshold instead
span.quote: For the purposes of survey research, the population of remote gig workers is an ambiguous concept, as people’s engagement with platforms varies from merely registering an account to earning a full-time income, and also changes over time.

span.label: the survey is used only to show that interview themes are shared more widely, not to estimate population quantities
span.quote: The survey results are used to demonstrate that themes developed from our interview informants’ experiences are also shared by many other remote gig workers in these countries.

span.label: research on remote gig work quality is limited in both the number of studies and the breadth of platforms and countries covered, which bounds what the findings can be compared against
span.quote: However, research on the quality of remote gig work remains limited, both in the number of studies undertaken and breadth of platforms and countries investigated

span.label: 40 of the 147 workers interviewed were excluded because they did not use either of the two platforms under study
span.note: eliminates: workers with no experience of the two platforms under study contributing to findings about those platforms - 40 of 147 interviewees were excluded on that ground · outcome: held
span.quote: In total 147 workers were interviewed, however, in the present analysis we exclude 40 workers who did not use either of the platforms discussed below.

span.label: 174 of 853 survey responses were excluded - wrong region, incomplete job-quality modules, or a failed attention check - leaving 679
span.note: eliminates: inattentive or mis-targeted responses as a source of the survey results - 174 of 853 were removed for wrong region, incomplete modules, or a failed attention check · outcome: held
span.quote: We obtained a total of 853 responses, of which 174 were excluded due to not being located in SEA or SSA, not having completed the modules related to job quality or failing an attention check. This left us with a sample of 679 workers, of which 40% were female and 60% male and 51% were located in SEA and 49% in SSA.

span.label: participants were told the interview was research and not a job, and that no platform feedback would be left either way - removing the reputational stake that would otherwise shape what a rated worker says
span.note: eliminates: the reputational stake as an influence on what workers said - participants were told it was research, not a job, and that no platform feedback would be left either way · outcome: held
span.quote: To further make that point, it was emphasised that no feedback would be left as an outcome of the participation.

span.label: purposive invitation across countries, genders and skills was used in place of an open task, which the authors argue mitigates self-selection on task-type preference and reservation wage
span.note: eliminates: self-selection on task-type preference and reservation wage, which an open posted task would have introduced - purposive invitation across countries, genders and skills was used instead · outcome: partial
span.quote: The result is likely to be more representative of the population than samples recruited simply by posting an open task because it mitigates self-selection biases from task type preferences and reservation wages.

span.label: algorithmic control
span.quote: Despite varying country contexts and types of work, we show that algorithmic control is central to the operation of online labour platforms. Algorithmic management techniques tend to offer workers high levels of flexibility, autonomy, task variety and complexity. However, these mechanisms of control can also result in low pay, social isolation, working unsocial and irregular hours, overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion.

span.label: algorithmic management
span.quote: This form of control differs significantly from the Taylorist control often attributed to the extensive use of informational management tools. In contrast to Taylorism, algorithmic management techniques enabled by platform-based rating and ranking systems facilitate high levels of autonomy, task variety and complexity, as well as potential spatial and temporal flexibility.

span.label: gig economy
span.quote: The review defined the gig economy as ‘people using apps \[also commonly known as platforms\] to sell their labour’

span.label: remote gig work
span.quote: Focusing on workers in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, the article draws on semi-structured interviews in six countries ( _N_ = 107) and a cross-regional survey ( _N_ = 679) to detail the manner in which remote gig work is shaped by platform-based algorithmic control.

span.label: job quality
span.quote: This article evaluates the job quality of work in the remote gig economy. Such work consists of the remote provision of a wide variety of digital services mediated by online labour platforms.

span.label: online labour platforms
span.quote: This article evaluates the job quality of work in the remote gig economy. Such work consists of the remote provision of a wide variety of digital services mediated by online labour platforms.

span.label: autonomy
span.quote: In terms of job quality, this entails a lack of worker autonomy combined with high levels of work intensity.

span.label: Taylorist
span.quote: This Taylorist informational control and discipline involves subjecting work tasks to detailed digital measurements and statistical analyses of individual worker performance.

span.label: work intensity
span.quote: In terms of job quality, this entails a lack of worker autonomy combined with high levels of work intensity.

span.label: symbolic power
span.quote: The identification of the ‘symbolic power’ ( Thompson, 1991) of platform reputations as an emerging form of marketplace bargaining power is an important contribution of this article.

span.label: marketplace bargaining power
span.quote: The identification of the ‘symbolic power’ ( Thompson, 1991) of platform reputations as an emerging form of marketplace bargaining power is an important contribution of this article.

span.label: structural power
span.quote: The autonomy resulting from algorithmic control can lead to overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion as a consequence of the weak structural power of workers vis-a-vis clients.

span.label: platform reputation
span.quote: In the case of remote gig work, the individual resources that we find to be most important are _skills_ and _platform reputation_. Workers lacking these individual resources suffered from low incomes and insecurity.

span.label: social isolation
span.quote: while algorithmic control provides remote gig workers with formal control over where they work, workers may have little real choice but to work from home, and this can lead to a lack of social contact and feelings of social isolation.

span.label: customer management
span.quote: Algorithmic management is an extension of ‘customer management’ strategies, which entails positioning customers ‘as agents in the management circuit’, so that ‘customers, rather than managers, are \[…\] the ones who must be pleased, whose orders must be followed, whose ideas, whims and desires appear to dictate how work is performed’

span.label: labour process
span.quote: What is notable about this algorithmic system of control in terms of job quality, compared to Taylorist forms of informational control, is that control operated at the end of the labour process rather than during it.

span.label: discretion
span.quote: This afforded workers freedom to work however they wished as long as the end product was accurate or satisfactory to the client. In effect, this organisational form afforded significant autonomy and discretion.

span.label: overwork
span.quote: The autonomy resulting from algorithmic control can lead to overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion as a consequence of the weak structural power of workers vis-a-vis clients.

span.label: non-proximity
span.quote: This weak structural power is an outcome of platform-based rating and ranking systems enabling a form of control which is able to overcome the spatial and temporal barriers that non-proximity places on the effectiveness of direct labour process surveillance and supervision.

span.label: theory elaboration
span.quote: These qualitative data were coded, following Vaughan’s (1992) theory elaboration approach. Initial codes were informed by the extant job quality literature and new codes developed out of an iterative process. Nvivo enabled systematic theoretical coding to be undertaken and hundreds of initial codes to be generated.

span.label: purposive
span.quote: The sampling strategy was purposive, the main aims being to ensure that workers had been active on one of two leading platforms for at least six months, that a diversity of work types were covered and that there was a rough gender balance.

span.label: self-selection biases
span.quote: The result is likely to be more representative of the population than samples recruited simply by posting an open task because it mitigates self-selection biases from task type preferences and reservation wages.

span.label: autonomy - IN THIS PAPER A REAL AND MEASURED FREEDOM THAT DOES NOT IMPLY GOOD WORK. 72% could choose the order of tasks and 74% their methods, and the same workers report overwork, sleep deprivation and exhaustion. The paper's whole argument is that autonomy and job quality come apart, so reading `autonomy` as a job-quality outcome inverts the finding
span.quote: This is echoed in our survey, where 72% of respondents felt able to choose and change the order in which they undertook online tasks, and 74% were able to choose or change their methods of work.

span.label: algorithmic control - CONTROL EXERCISED AT THE END OF THE LABOUR PROCESS RATHER THAN DURING IT. That single structural fact generates the whole pattern: because only the output is judged, the worker is free in how they work, and because the rating governs future work, the freedom is unusable
span.quote: What is notable about this algorithmic system of control in terms of job quality, compared to Taylorist forms of informational control, is that control operated at the end of the labour process rather than during it.

span.label: algorithmic management - NOT SUPERVISION BY MACHINE BUT CUSTOMER MANAGEMENT EXTENDED: the client is placed in the management circuit, and the platform's ranking turns their rating into a sanction. The controller is another user, not an algorithm with a policy
span.quote: Algorithmic management is an extension of ‘customer management’ strategies, which entails positioning customers ‘as agents in the management circuit’, so that ‘customers, rather than managers, are \[…\] the ones who must be pleased, whose orders must be followed, whose ideas, whims and desires appear to dictate how work is performed’

span.label: platform reputation - AN INDIVIDUAL RESOURCE IN THE LABOUR MARKET, alongside skills, rather than a signal about past work. It is what the paper means by reputation having `symbolic power`: it is held by the worker, cannot be transferred between platforms, and determines what work is reachable at all
span.quote: In the case of remote gig work, the individual resources that we find to be most important are _skills_ and _platform reputation_. Workers lacking these individual resources suffered from low incomes and insecurity.

span.label: contradicts → accounts which hold that ICTs bring Taylorist organisational forms to white-collar work - the 'assembly line in the head' and 'electronic sweatshop' readings - which this study's remote gig workers do not fit
span.quote: Thus remote gig work is a long way from being an ‘assembly line in the head’ ( Bain and Taylor, 2000) or ‘electronic sweatshop’

span.label: contradicts → Shapiro's characterisation of gig-work autonomy as 'autonomy over minute decisions', which the authors find far from minute for remote gig work
span.quote: Shapiro (2017) refers to the autonomy of local gig workers over things such as when to work and which orders to accept or reject as only constituting ‘autonomy over minute decisions’. Yet our findings suggest that for remote gig workers the level of discretion is far from minute.

span.label: extends → Silver's and Wright's concept of marketplace bargaining power, which this article extends with a symbolic form neither of them considers
span.quote: Marketplace bargaining power is a concept developed by Silver (2003) and Wright (2000), neither of whom consider the importance of symbolic forms of power.

span.label: qualifies → the literature on Taylorist informational control, which is predominantly based on call-centre research and was generalised into theories of effort-biased technology adoption
span.quote: Accounts of Taylorist informational control are predominately based on research in call centres. However, this research has informed more general theories regarding the adoption of technology being ‘effort biased’

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1177/0950017018785616.
